The world trading system is more turbulent, uncertain and challenging, but New Zealand is well placed to navigate this new world trade disorder.\n\nWe will, however, need to double-down on three inter-connected ‘pillars’ of trade policy: rules; resilience and innovation.\n\nIn his presentation, Vangelis Vitalis will explain what this means and how it can help us 'prevent the jungle from growing back'.\n\nWhen: Tuesday 30 June 2026, 10:30am-12:00pm NZST\nWhere: The Treasury, Level 3, 1 The Terrace, Wellington, and also online\n\nYou can register for in-person attendance at https://lnkd.in/dm4TrhX8\n\nTo register for virtual attendance, visit https://lnkd.in/dgn38hk8","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/new-zealand-treasury_treasury-guest-lecture-with-vangelis-vitalis-activity-7467800294941306881-398i"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"The Treasury - New Zealand","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/new-zealand-treasury"},"datePublished":"2026-06-01T22:25:23.743Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/new-zealand-treasury_budget-2026-28-may-2026-activity-7467340550904459264-PCjy","text":"The Minister of Finance, Hon Nicola Willis, delivered Budget 2026 on 28 May, alongside the Treasury’s Budget Economic and Fiscal Update 2026 (BEFU).\n\nThe Budget outlines how much money the Government expects to receive over the coming financial year, and how and on what it plans to spend it. Come along in person or join us online to here Luiz de Mello talk about \"Reinforcing resilience while maintaining efficiency: A practical strategy for New Zealand in a shock prone world\".\n\nWhen: Friday 8 May 2026, 10:00am-11:30am NZST\nWhere: The Treasury, Level 3, 1 The Terrace, Wellington, and online\n\nAbout this lecture:\n\nNew Zealand’s economic framework has long emphasised macroeconomic stability, openness, and efficiency. These settings have supported growth and institutional credibility. However, recent global shocks, including supply chain distribution disruption, energy volatility, and geopolitical uncertainty, have highlighted the importance of economic resilience alongside efficiency.\n\nNew Zealand's macroeconomic framework, characterized by low public debt, a credible monetary policy regime, and strong fiscal institutions, provides capacity to respond to shocks. However, the microeconomic structure of the economy has increasingly been optimised for efficiency, with limited redundancy in key areas such as energy, trade, and supply chains.\n\nUsing illustrative examples, including dependence on imported liquid fuels, the lecture examines how structural features can amplify the impact of external shocks at the sector level. It then considers how microeconomic resilience can complement existing macroeconomic strengths. Drawing on OECD analysis and international experience, the lecture outlines an industrial policy approach focused on addressing coordination failures, improving diffusion of technology, and strengthening economic ecosystems, rather than selecting firms or sectors. It highlights practical, low-cost policy levers that support adaptability and a small, open economy.\n\nTo register for virtual attendance, go to https://lnkd.in/eqGz-But\n\nTo register for in-person attendance, visit https://lnkd.in/e7z8t2ZF","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/new-zealand-treasury_treasury-guest-lecture-with-luiz-de-mello-activity-7457627242442129408-Wgwh"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"The Treasury - New Zealand","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/new-zealand-treasury"},"datePublished":"2026-05-05T01:54:47.104Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/new-zealand-treasury_treasury-guest-lecture-with-phil-oreilly-activity-7457246385025794048--NzY","text":"We are delighted to host Phil O'Reilly ONZM next week as part of the Treasury Guest Lecture Series.\n\nWhen:  Wednesday 13 May 2026, 10:30am-12:00pm NZST\nWhere: The Treasury, Level 3, 1 The Terrace, Wellington, or join us online\n\nHere's what to expect:\n\n\"Changes in the global order are leading to changes in global business priorities. But some things don’t change: Business still seeks a competitive, level playing field and access to markets.\n\nThe world is reglobalising, not deglobalising, and that is creating new opportunities for New Zealand businesses. Markets that were once thought of as difficult to access are now open for business. Relationships once thought moribund are now reinvigorated.\n\nDespite the doomsayers, New Zealand can arguably look with real confidence to the world we see emerging. But we need to understand those new opportunities and the new rules of the game.\n\nThe emergence of industry policy and an increased focus on defence and critical minerals with national resilience at the core are just some of the trends at national level. And globally, we need to vigorously engage in the future of multilateral institutions that have been so important to us for decades.\n\nAll of these changes are a potential opportunity for us, if only we can grasp them.\n\nThe risk is that we continue to see the world through old eyes. That we fail to critique old policy settings and be self-critical of our existing beliefs about what makes New Zealand an attractive place to do business. New Zealand","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/new-zealand-treasury"},"datePublished":"2026-04-22T23:59:09.571Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/new-zealand-treasury_treasury-guest-lecture-with-professor-prasanna-activity-7452868632612823041-mR44","text":"We have another terrific and topical guest lecture coming up soon - \"Shipping Lanes and Inflation-at-Risk: Hub Shocks and Optimal Monetary Policy\" from Prasanna Gai, Professor of Macroeconomics at the University of Auckland.\n\nPrasanna Gai will look at how disruptions to key supply‑chain hubs, like energy and shipping routes, can turn into broad inflation risks. When these hubs are hit, costs rise across the economy, but so does uncertainty about how long inflation will last. Firms’ expectations start to move together, and that makes extreme inflation outcomes more likely — even if the average outlook doesn’t shift much.\n\nWhen: Monday 4 May, 1:30-3:00pm NZST\nWhere: The Treasury, Level 3, 1 The Terrace, Wellington, and also online\n\nTo register for in-person attendance, please go to https://lnkd.in/eHjXYJRS\n\nTo register for online attendance, visit https://lnkd.in/eAJXdSuD","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/new-zealand-treasury_treasury-guest-lecture-with-professor-prasanna-activity-7452868632612823041-mR44"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"The Treasury - New Zealand","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/new-zealand-treasury"},"datePublished":"2026-04-20T22:06:11.867Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/new-zealand-treasury_treasury-guest-lecture-with-dr-alan-bollard-activity-7452115429059301376-lJEP","text":"We have a very timely guest lecture next week from former Treasury Secretary and respected economist, director and academic, Dr Alan Bollard.         " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Today, the Government has released its formal response to the National Infrastructure Plan. This marks a new phase for New Zealand’s infrastructure system.

When we published the Plan earlier this year, we said New Zealand needed to do things differently to deliver the infrastructure we need to thrive over the next 30 years.

The Government’s response today, accepting the case for change and confirming the direction of reform, is a step in the right direction in improving performance and getting better value for money from our infrastructure.
The response formally addresses each of the 16 recommendations and 10 priority areas in the Plan. Thirteen of the 16 recommendations are fully supported and the remaining three supported in principle. Action on some of the recommendations is already underway.

Work with the Treasury is being undertaken to build a new assurance process for central government infrastructure investment. This will be in place on 1 November.

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">We are looking forward to our next Treasury guest lecture by <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/mfatnz?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>New Zealand Ministry of Foreign Affairs & Trade</a> Deputy Secretary Vangelis Vitalis on the topic 'The international context for New Zealand trade policy – where we were and where we are – and how do we respond?'

The golden weather for New Zealand trade policy - from 1995 to roughly 2017 - is well and truly over. The world trading system is more turbulent, uncertain and challenging, but New Zealand is well placed to navigate this new world trade disorder.

We will, however, need to double-down on three inter-connected ‘pillars’ of trade policy: rules; resilience and innovation.

In his presentation, Vangelis Vitalis will explain what this means and how it can help us 'prevent the jungle from growing back'.

When: Tuesday 30 June 2026, 10:30am-12:00pm NZST
Where: The Treasury, Level 3, 1 The Terrace, Wellington, and also online

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">We will be ending this week on a great note with a guest lecture by <a class="link" href="https://fr.linkedin.com/in/luiz-de-mello-aa9a167?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Luiz de Mello</a>, Director of the Country Studies Branch at the Economics Department of the OECD. Come along in person or join us online to here Luiz de Mello talk about "Reinforcing resilience while maintaining efficiency: A practical strategy for New Zealand in a shock prone world".

When: Friday 8 May 2026, 10:00am-11:30am NZST
Where: The Treasury, Level 3, 1 The Terrace, Wellington, and online

About this lecture:

New Zealand’s economic framework has long emphasised macroeconomic stability, openness, and efficiency. These settings have supported growth and institutional credibility. However, recent global shocks, including supply chain distribution disruption, energy volatility, and geopolitical uncertainty, have highlighted the importance of economic resilience alongside efficiency.

New Zealand's macroeconomic framework, characterized by low public debt, a credible monetary policy regime, and strong fiscal institutions, provides capacity to respond to shocks. However, the microeconomic structure of the economy has increasingly been optimised for efficiency, with limited redundancy in key areas such as energy, trade, and supply chains.

Using illustrative examples, including dependence on imported liquid fuels, the lecture examines how structural features can amplify the impact of external shocks at the sector level. It then considers how microeconomic resilience can complement existing macroeconomic strengths. Drawing on OECD analysis and international experience, the lecture outlines an industrial policy approach focused on addressing coordination failures, improving diffusion of technology, and strengthening economic ecosystems, rather than selecting firms or sectors. It highlights practical, low-cost policy levers that support adaptability and a small, open economy.

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">We are delighted to host <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/in/phil-o-reilly?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Phil O'Reilly ONZM</a> next week as part of the Treasury Guest Lecture Series.

When:  Wednesday 13 May 2026, 10:30am-12:00pm NZST
Where: The Treasury, Level 3, 1 The Terrace, Wellington, or join us online

Here's what to expect:

"Changes in the global order are leading to changes in global business priorities. But some things don’t change: Business still seeks a competitive, level playing field and access to markets.

The world is reglobalising, not deglobalising, and that is creating new opportunities for New Zealand businesses. Markets that were once thought of as difficult to access are now open for business. Relationships once thought moribund are now reinvigorated.

Despite the doomsayers, New Zealand can arguably look with real confidence to the world we see emerging. But we need to understand those new opportunities and the new rules of the game.

The emergence of industry policy and an increased focus on defence and critical minerals with national resilience at the core are just some of the trends at national level. And globally, we need to vigorously engage in the future of multilateral institutions that have been so important to us for decades.

All of these changes are a potential opportunity for us, if only we can grasp them.

The risk is that we continue to see the world through old eyes. That we fail to critique old policy settings and be self-critical of our existing beliefs about what makes New Zealand an attractive place to do business. And worst of all, that business just leaves it to Government to do all the thinking."

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">We have another terrific and topical guest lecture coming up soon - "Shipping Lanes and Inflation-at-Risk: Hub Shocks and Optimal Monetary Policy" from Prasanna Gai, Professor of Macroeconomics at the University of Auckland.

Prasanna Gai will look at how disruptions to key supply‑chain hubs, like energy and shipping routes, can turn into broad inflation risks. When these hubs are hit, costs rise across the economy, but so does uncertainty about how long inflation will last. Firms’ expectations start to move together, and that makes extreme inflation outcomes more likely — even if the average outlook doesn’t shift much.

When: Monday 4 May, 1:30-3:00pm NZST
Where: The Treasury, Level 3, 1 The Terrace, Wellington, and also online
